html:
Maroons were Africans and their descendants in the Americas who escaped slavery and built free communities of their own, usually in mountains, swamps or forests out of reach of the plantations. The name comes from the Spanish cimarrón, "wild" or "runaway".

Wherever the Atlantic slave trade brought people, some ran away. Many maroon communities were small and short-lived, but some became real states that fought colonial armies to a standstill:

  • Palmares in north east Brazil held out for most of the 1600s, until it was destroyed in 1694.
  • In Jamaica the Maroons of the mountains fought the British until treaties in 1739 and 1740 recognised their freedom and land.
  • In Surinam, later called Dutch Guiana, the Saramaka, Ndyuka and other peoples won treaties of freedom from the Dutch in the 1760s. They kept their own languages, religion and government in the rainforest, and today they are a large part of the population of Suriname.
  • San Basilio de Palenque in Colombia won its freedom from Spain in the early 1700s.

Maroons often traded with, fought or married into Indigenous peoples. Their communities were a constant threat to slave societies, and in many places their descendants still hold land and identity as Maroons.
